title: Nullable value semantics — in-band sentinels + null-fallback arithmetic
body:
## What it is

A value can be present or absent. An absent value is `null`. Doing arithmetic with a `null` simply produces `null` again instead of stopping your program.

## How it aids you

Missing data — a lookup that found nothing, a field never filled in — no longer has to be a special case that crashes. The absence flows through your calculation as `null`, so you can carry on and decide what to do about it at the end rather than guarding every step.

## Example

```loft
fn main() {
    a = null as integer;   // a holds no value
    b = a + 10;            // arithmetic on null gives null, no crash
    println("{a} {b}");    // null null
    println("still running");
}
```

title: `??` null-coalescing operator (incl. `?? return`)
body:
## What it is

The `??` operator supplies a fallback: `value ?? fallback` gives you `value` when it has one, and `fallback` when `value` is null.

## How it aids you

It turns "this might be missing" into "here is a sensible default" in a single, readable step — no `if`-checks around every optional value. You state the backup once, right where the value is used.

## Example

```loft
fn main() {
    missing = null as integer;
    count = missing ?? 0;       // use 0 when the value is null
    name = "Ada" ?? "unknown";  // keeps the real value when present
    println("{count} {name}");  // 0 Ada
}
```

title: Primitive scalar types (integer, float, single, boolean, character)
Ranged/width integer types (u8/i8/u16/i16/i32/u32)
body:
## What it is

Besides the everyday `integer`, loft offers smaller number types sized to their range: `u8`, `i8`, `u16`, `i16`, `i32`, `u32`. Each holds whole numbers within fixed bounds and takes up less space.

## How it aids you

When you store many numbers you know stay small — a colour channel (0..255), an age, a year — these compact types keep your data small and your intent clear, while you still write and read them like ordinary numbers.

## Example

```loft
fn main() {
    level: u8 = 200;      // fits in a single byte (0..255)
    year: u16 = 2026;     // fits in two bytes
    temp: i8 = -40;       // small signed value
    println("{level} {year} {temp}");   // 200 2026 -40
}
```

title: Type conversions — implicit, format-only, and explicit `as`
body:
## What it is

The `as` cast converts a value from one type to another on purpose: `pi as integer`, `"42" as integer`, `'A' as integer`. You ask for the conversion, so it happens exactly where you write it.

## How it aids you

You get to move between types deliberately — round a decimal down to a whole number, read a number out of text, get a character's code — with the conversion visible in the code. Nothing silently changes type behind your back.

## Example

```loft
fn main() {
    pi: float = 3.75;
    whole = pi as integer;     // 3  (drops the fraction)
    parsed = "42" as integer;  // text turned into a number
    code = 'A' as integer;     // 65 (the character's code)
    println("{whole} {parsed} {code}");   // 3 42 65
}
```

body:
## What it is

Pass a function's arguments by name — `connect(host: "db", port: 5432)` — instead of only in order, and give parameters default values so callers can leave them out.

## How it aids you

Call sites read like their own documentation, and you can set just the one option you care about without listing everything before it. Adding a new optional setting later never breaks the calls people already wrote.

## Example

```loft
fn connect(host: text, port: integer = 8080, tls: boolean = true) -> text {
    "{host}:{port} tls={tls}"
}
fn main() {
    println(connect("example.com"));              // example.com:8080 tls=true
    println(connect("example.com", tls: false));  // example.com:8080 tls=false
    println(connect(host: "db", port: 5432));     // db:5432 tls=true
}
```

body:
## What it is

When a calculation cannot give a real answer — a number grows too big to hold, or you divide by zero — loft produces `null` for that result and keeps running, instead of crashing.

## How it aids you

One bad calculation no longer takes down the whole program. The trouble spot becomes a `null` you can spot and handle (often with `??` to supply a fallback), the way a spreadsheet shows an error in one cell while the rest of the sheet still works.

## Example

```loft
fn main() {
    big: integer = 9_000_000_000_000_000_000;
    total = big + big;          // overflow -> null, no crash
    println("{total}");         // null
    divisor: integer = 0;
    safe = 100 / divisor ?? -1; // divide by zero -> null -> fallback
    println("{safe}");          // -1
    println("done");            // program keeps running
}
```

title: Math & trigonometry library
body:
## What it is

A set of ready-made number functions: absolute value, the smaller or larger of two values (`min` / `max`), square root, powers (`pow`), the trigonometry functions (`sin` / `cos` / `tan`), rounding (`floor` / `ceil` / `round`), logarithms, and the constant `PI`.

## How it aids you

Reach for the operation you need by name instead of spelling out the formula by hand — one call for a square root, a power, or an angle — so numeric code stays short and reads the way you would say it out loud.

## Example

```loft
fn main() {
    println("abs: {abs(-7)}");            // abs: 7
    println("min/max: {min(3, 9)} {max(3, 9)}");  // min/max: 3 9
    println("sqrt: {sqrt(144.0)}");       // sqrt: 12
    println("pow: {pow(2.0, 10.0)}");     // pow: 1024
    println("cos(0): {cos(0.0)}");        // cos(0): 1
    println("pi: {PI}");                  // pi: 3.141592653589793
}
```

title: File & directory I/O (+ durable-store binding)
Environment & arguments (env vars, arguments(), program dirs, path resolution)
JSON — json_parse, JsonValue, Type.parse, to_json
body:
## What it is

Turn JSON text into a value with `json_parse(...)`, then read from it: `field(name)` for an object member, `item(index)` for a list entry, and `as_text` / `as_long` / `as_number` / `as_bool` to get a plain value back. `len()` counts a list, and there are matching builders (`json_object`, `json_array`, `json_string`, ...) plus `to_json()` to produce JSON text.

## How it aids you

Work with config files and web responses directly — ask for a field by name or an item by position and get it back in the type you expect — instead of picking the raw text apart yourself.

## Example

```loft
fn main() {
    raw = "{{\"name\": \"loft\", \"version\": 2, \"tags\": [\"fast\", \"typed\"]}}";
    doc = json_parse(raw);
    println("name: {doc.field("name").as_text()}");        // name: loft
    println("version: {doc.field("version").as_long()}");  // version: 2
    println("first tag: {doc.field("tags").item(0).as_text()}");  // first tag: fast
    println("tag count: {doc.field("tags").len()}");       // tag count: 2
}
```

title: Logging & diagnostics API (log_*, print, assert, panic)
`sizeof()`
body:
## What it is

`sizeof(...)` tells you how many bytes a type or value takes up when it is packed for storage — for a built-in type, one of your own structs, or a variable.

## How it aids you

Know the storage footprint of your data before you write it out — useful when you save records to a file or reason about how much space a large collection will need.

## Example

```loft
struct Point { x: integer, y: integer }

fn main() {
    println("integer: {sizeof(integer)}");  // integer: 8
    println("u8: {sizeof(u8)}");            // u8: 1
    println("u16: {sizeof(u16)}");          // u16: 2
    println("Point: {sizeof(Point)}");      // Point: 16
}
```

title: Type aliases (`type X = …`)
Library imports / module system (`use` forms, `pub`)
body:
## What it is

`use` brings names — functions and types — from another `.loft` file or an installed library into your file, so you can call them directly. Put `use` lines at the top of the file.

## How it aids you

Split a program across files and pull in shared code — your own helpers or a published library — without copying it, so each file stays focused and the same code is written once and reused.

## Example

Two files side by side. `greetlib.loft` offers a public function; `main.loft` imports it:

```loft
// greetlib.loft
pub fn greet(name: text) -> text {
    "hello, {name}"
}
```

```loft
// main.loft  — imports greet from greetlib
use greetlib::greet;

fn main() {
    println(greet("loft"));   // hello, loft
}
```

The common forms of `use`:

```loft
use mathlib;                 // bring in every public name
use mathlib::sqrt;           // bring in just one name
use mathlib::(sqrt, pow);    // bring in several (parentheses required)
use mathlib::sqrt as root;   // rename on import
use mathlib as m;            // reach names as m::sqrt
```

title: The `loft` CLI — run a program, `--interpret` / `--native`, `--timeout`, `--help`
body:
## What it is

The `loft` command runs a program written in loft. Point it at a source file and it compiles and runs the program in one step. By default it builds a fast native binary; `--interpret` runs the program through the built-in interpreter instead. `--timeout` caps how long a run may take, and `--help` lists everything the command can do.

## How it aids you

One command takes you from a `.loft` file to a running program — there is no separate build or install step to manage. You switch between the quick-starting interpreter and the faster native build with a single flag, and `--timeout` stops a runaway program instead of letting it tie up your terminal.

## Example

```
$ loft hello.loft                 # compile and run (native backend, the default)
Hello, world!

$ loft --interpret hello.loft     # run through the interpreter instead
Hello, world!

$ loft --timeout 60 slow.loft     # hard-kill the run after 60 seconds (0 = no limit)

$ loft --help                     # list every option and subcommand
```

title: REPL — interactive sessions
body:
## What it is

An interactive session you start with `loft repl` (or just `loft` with no file). You type loft one line at a time and see each result straight away. It reopens your last session automatically; `loft repl --fresh` starts from a clean slate.

## How it aids you

You can try an expression, check what a function returns, or shape a struct without writing a whole program first. Whatever you define — variables, functions, types — stays available for the rest of the session, so you build an idea up step by step. It is the quickest way to answer "what does this do?".

## Example

```
$ loft repl
loft REPL — :help for commands, :quit to exit
loft> x = 40 + 2
loft> x
42
loft> fn dbl(n: integer) -> integer { n + n }
loft> dbl(x)
84
loft> :quit
```

title: Introspection — `loft introspect` (bytecode / native Rust / slot tables)
body:
## What it is

`loft introspect prog.loft` shows you how loft sees your program: the bytecode the interpreter runs, the Rust source the native backend generates, the stack-slot layout, and the resolved types. By default it prints every section; flags like `--show-bytecode`, `--show-rust`, or `--fn <name>` narrow it down.

## How it aids you

It turns "what is the compiler actually doing with my code?" into something you can read. When a program behaves unexpectedly, or you want to understand the cost of a construct, you can look straight at the generated code instead of guessing. `--fn` focuses on a single function so you are not wading through the whole program.

## Example

```
$ loft introspect prog.loft                   # bytecode + generated Rust + slots + types

$ loft introspect --show-bytecode prog.loft   # just the bytecode section
$ loft introspect --show-rust prog.loft       # just the generated Rust
$ loft introspect --fn main prog.loft         # only the function `main`
```

title: Debugger — breakpoints, frame capture, scripted RPC
body:
## What it is

`loft debug prog.loft:12` runs your program and pauses it at line 12, dropping you into an interactive `(dbg)` prompt. From there you inspect variables (type a name to see its value), advance one line at a time with `:step` / `:next`, resume with `:continue`, and leave with `:quit`.

## How it aids you

Instead of scattering print statements through your code and re-running, you stop the program where it matters and look at the real values in the live frame. You can watch state change line by line, which makes it far easier to see where a result first goes wrong.

## Example

```
$ loft debug prog.loft:12
loft debugger — break at prog.loft:12.  :help for commands, :continue to run, :quit to exit
(dbg) total          # inspect a local by name
42
(dbg) :step          # run the next line
(dbg) :continue      # resume until the program ends
(dbg) :quit
```

title: Source formatter — canonical `.loft` output
body:
## What it is

A built-in source formatter. `loft --format file.loft` rewrites the file in canonical loft style in place; `loft --format-check file.loft` leaves the file alone and just exits non-zero if it is not already formatted. `loft --format -` reads from standard input and writes the result to standard output.

## How it aids you

Everyone's loft looks the same, so you never argue about spacing or indentation and diffs stay small and meaningful. `--format-check` plugs into a commit hook or CI to keep a whole project consistent automatically, and the `-` form lets an editor format a file or selection on demand.

## Example

```
$ loft --format main.loft          # reformat the file in place

$ loft --format-check main.loft    # exit 1 if it is not already canonical (for CI)

$ cat main.loft | loft --format -  # format from stdin to stdout
```

title: Native-binary backend (`--native` → rustc)
body:
## What it is

The native backend. `loft --native prog.loft` translates your program to Rust and compiles it with `rustc` into a real machine-code binary, then runs it. It is already the default when you run `loft prog.loft`; `--native-release` builds an optimised binary, and `--native-emit` writes out the generated Rust for you to keep.

## How it aids you

You get compiled-language speed from the same source you were interpreting, with no rewrite and no separate toolchain to wire up. Reach for `--native-release` when you want the fastest possible run, and use `--native-emit` when you want to see or reuse the Rust that loft produced.

## Example

```
$ loft --native prog.loft          # compile via rustc and run (this is the default)

$ loft --native-release prog.loft  # optimised build (rustc -O), for benchmarking

$ loft --native-emit prog.loft     # write the generated Rust and exit (no run)
```

title: Browser / WASM target (`--html` / `--native-wasm`)
body:
## What it is

The browser target. `loft --html prog.loft` compiles your program to WebAssembly and bundles it into a single self-contained HTML file you can open in any browser. `loft --native-wasm prog.loft` emits just the `.wasm` module when you want to embed it yourself.

## How it aids you

The same loft program that runs on your machine can run on a web page, with nothing to install for whoever opens it — one HTML file is the whole deliverable. It is the simplest way to share a demo, a tool, or a game that people can try with a single click.

## Example

```
$ loft --html game.loft            # write a self-contained game.html
$ # open game.html in a browser — no server or install needed

$ loft --native-wasm game.loft     # emit just game.wasm to embed yourself
```

title: Package management (`loft install`, `loft.toml`, lockfile)
body:
## What it is

loft's package manager. `loft install <name>` downloads a library from the registry and installs it for use; a `loft.toml` file records the packages your project depends on, and a lockfile pins the exact versions so builds stay reproducible. `loft new <name>` scaffolds a fresh library, and `loft update` refreshes the pinned versions.

## How it aids you

You reuse other people's libraries instead of reinventing them, and the lockfile means the versions you tested are the versions everyone else — and your CI — gets. Declaring dependencies in `loft.toml` keeps a project's requirements in one place that travels with the code.

## Example

```
$ loft new mytool                  # scaffold loft.toml + src/ + tests/
$ loft install markdown            # fetch a library from the registry
$ loft install markdown@1.2.0      # or pin a specific version
$ loft update                      # refresh the lockfile to the latest allowed versions
```

title: Live code reload — patch a running program
body:
## What it is

Live code reload. With reload enabled, loft watches your source file while the program runs and swaps in edited functions on the fly, so your changes take effect without stopping and restarting the program. It is opt-in via the `LOFT_LIVE_RELOAD` setting.

## How it aids you

You keep the program's current state — the game you are part-way through, the data you loaded, the window you opened — and still see code edits apply immediately. That tightens the edit-and-see loop and removes the restart-and-get-back-to-where-you-were tax when you are iterating on behaviour.

## Example

```
$ LOFT_LIVE_RELOAD=1 loft game.loft
# the program keeps running; edit and save game.loft in your editor…
# …the changed functions are hot-swapped into the live program automatically
```

title: Lexer
body:
## What it does

Turns raw loft source text into a stream of tokens — keywords, names, numbers, operators, punctuation — that the parser can consume. It is the first stage of the pipeline and handles character-level details such as comments, string literals, and string interpolation, so later stages never touch raw text.

## Where it lives

`src/lexer.rs`

title: Parser (two-pass recursive descent)
body:
## What it does

Reads the lexer's tokens and builds the program's intermediate representation (IR) using a two-pass recursive-descent grammar: a first pass registers every definition (types, functions), so a second pass can resolve references regardless of the order they appear in the source. This is where loft syntax becomes a structured tree.

## Where it lives

`src/parser/` (entry point `src/parser/mod.rs`)

title: Type resolver
body:
## What it does

Resolves every type name to a concrete definition and works out each type's memory layout — its size and the byte offset of each field. This gives the rest of the compiler the fixed shapes it needs to lay out values and to generate field access.

## Where it lives

`src/typedef.rs`

title: Scope & dependency/lifetime tracker (deps)
body:
## What it does

Tracks which names are visible in each scope and follows how values borrow from and depend on one another, so the compiler knows when each value can safely be freed. This dependency ("deps") information is the backbone of loft's ownership and memory-safety model.

## Where it lives

`src/scopes.rs`

title: Stack slot allocator
body:
## What it does

Assigns each local variable and temporary a fixed slot on the runtime stack, deciding the layout of every function's stack frame. Stable slot numbers let both the interpreter and the native backend read and write locals by position.

## Where it lives

`src/variables/` (entry point `src/variables/mod.rs`)

title: IR data model (Value/Type/Data)
body:
## What it does

Defines the core data types the whole compiler passes around: `Value` (an IR node), `Type` (a static type), and `Data` (the table of all named definitions). It is the shared vocabulary that the parser produces and every later stage consumes.

## Where it lives

`src/data.rs`

title: Store-resident IR (reader + handle + materializer)
body:
## What it does

Provides a form of the IR that lives directly in the word-addressed store, along with the reader, handle, and materializer used to access it. This lets a program's definitions be persisted and loaded without rebuilding them from source each time.

## Where it lives

`src/data_store.rs`

title: Bytecode compiler (IR -> bytecode)
body:
## What it does

Lowers the parser's tree-shaped IR into a flat stream of bytecode instructions for the interpreter, and initialises the native-function registry. It is the bridge between the structured IR and the linear form the VM executes.

## Where it lives

`src/compile.rs`

title: Bytecode code generator
body:
## What it does

Emits the individual bytecode instructions during compilation — the routines that decide which opcodes and operands represent each expression and statement. It is the writing end of the bytecode pipeline that the VM later reads.

## Where it lives

`src/state/codegen.rs`

title: Bytecode VM / executor
body:
## What it does

The virtual machine that runs the compiled bytecode: it holds the instruction stream and the runtime stack and drives the main execute loop that steps through opcodes. This is the engine of the interpreter backend.

## Where it lives

`src/state/mod.rs` (the `State` type and its execute loop)

title: Opcode implementations
body:
## What it does

Holds the actual behaviour of each bytecode operation — the per-opcode routines the VM dispatches to for arithmetic, comparisons, text and collection operations, and the rest. The file is generated from the `#rust"..."` operator templates in the standard library.

## Where it lives

`src/fill.rs`

title: Native Rust generator
body:
## What it does

The `--native` backend: translates the program's IR into Rust source code, which `rustc` then compiles into a fast standalone binary. It produces the same behaviour as the interpreter along a different, compile-to-machine-code path.

## Where it lives

`src/generation/` (entry point `src/generation/mod.rs`)

title: Word-addressed store
body:
## What it does

The raw heap: a flat, word-addressed block of memory that holds every value's bytes. Higher layers place records and collections into it and reference them by position. It is the lowest level of loft's memory model.

## Where it lives

`src/store.rs`

title: Database — alloc / persistence / journal / snapshot / schema
body:
## What it does

Manages all of a program's stores together with their schema, and provides allocation, persistence, journaling, and snapshotting on top of the raw heap. It is what makes loft's heap durable and recoverable rather than purely in-memory.

## Where it lives

`src/database/` (entry point `src/database/mod.rs`)

title: DbRef pointers & collection keys
body:
## What it does

Defines `DbRef`, loft's universal pointer — a triple of store number, record, and position that locates any value in the store — together with the key types used to index collections. Everything that refers to heap data does so through these.

## Where it lives

`src/keys.rs`

title: Parallel execution runtime
body:
## What it does

Runs loft's parallel constructs (parallel loops and tasks) across multiple threads, coordinating the work and access to the shared store safely. It is the machinery behind the language's `par` features.

## Where it lives

`src/parallel.rs`

title: Native function registry
body:
## What it does

Registers the built-in ("native") functions and methods — the parts of the standard library backed by Rust — and maps each loft-level name to its Rust implementation, so both backends can call it.

## Where it lives

`src/native.rs`

title: CDylib extension loader
body:
## What it does

Loads compiled native extension libraries (cdylibs) at runtime and connects their exported functions into the running program, letting a loft program call into prebuilt native code.

## Where it lives

`src/extensions.rs`

title: Diagnostics collector
body:
## What it does

Gathers the errors and warnings produced across the compiler stages and holds them in one place, so they can be reported to the user consistently with source locations attached.

## Where it lives

`src/diagnostics.rs`

title: Logger runtime
body:
## What it does

Implements the runtime logging system — the machinery behind loft's log and diagnostic output and the `LOFT_LOG` controls — routing messages to the right destinations at the configured verbosity.

## Where it lives

`src/logger.rs`

title: Registry / manifest / lockfile resolution
body:
## What it does

Resolves package dependencies for the package manager: it reads each project's manifest (`loft.toml`), consults the registry, and computes the lockfile that pins exact versions. It is the dependency-resolution brain behind `loft install`.

## Where it lives

`src/registry.rs`

title: Live-reload dispatch
body:
## What it does

The mechanism behind live code reload: it watches the source and, when a function changes, swaps the new version into the already-running program without a restart.

## Where it lives

`src/live_reload.rs`

title: Documentation generator (maintainer tooling)
body:
## What it does

Maintainer tooling that generates the project's HTML documentation from the source and standard library (the `gendoc` binary), keeping the published docs in sync with the code.

## Where it lives

`src/gendoc.rs`

title: Tracker indexer (maintainer tooling)
body:
## What it does

Maintainer tooling that scans the repository for `@`-prefixed tracker tags and builds the index that `scripts/idx` queries (`index/tags.json`). It is itself written in loft.

## Where it lives

`tools/indexer/` (scanner `tools/indexer/src/scan.loft`, query CLI `tools/indexer/src/idx.loft`)

title: Feature-catalogue sync generator (issues → in-project mirror + example tests)
body:
## What it does

Keeps the in-project copy of the feature catalogue in step with this issue tracker. It reads a committed snapshot of the issues and regenerates, one-way, a browsable mirror of every entry plus a runnable test file for each feature's example. Agents and CI then work from the issues without anything being written down twice: the issue is the single source, and two guards keep the copy honest — one fails if the mirror drifts from the snapshot, the other fails if any extracted example stops running.

## Where it lives

`tools/features/gen.loft` (the generator), the `Makefile` targets `features-fetch` / `features-gen` / `features-check`, and the example-runs guards in `tests/features.rs` (interpret) and `tests/native.rs::native_features` (native). Realizes strand 3 of @PLN92.
